== Biography ==

[[Glasgow-1076|Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan]] was born at Kilbirnie, Ayrshire, on 15 October 1747, the son of [[Glasgow-1075|Robert Glasgow]] and [[Allan-4046|Margaret Allan]]. The parish register records his baptism on 18 October.<ref name="birth">Kilbirnie Parish, Church of Scotland, ''Old Parish Registers Births and Baptisms'', National Records of Scotland, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk ScotlandsPeople], Robert Glasgow, 18 October 1747, Ref. 10/116, parish 596; transcribed on the WikiTree profile as “Robert laul son to Robert Glasgow of Puddevenholm & Margaret Allan.”</ref>

He married [[Dunlop-2189|Rachel Dunlop]] at Dunlop, Ayrshire, on 23 February 1802.<ref name="marriage">Dunlop Parish, Church of Scotland, ''Old Parish Registers Banns and Marriages'', National Records of Scotland, [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk ScotlandsPeople], Robert Glasgow and Rachel Dunlop, 23 February 1802, Ref. 20/211, parish 591.</ref>

Glasgow owned the Mount Grenan and Sans Souci estates on St Vincent. Simon D. Smith identifies finance from Houstoun & Co, his 1802 purchase of Montgreenan in Ayrshire, and construction of the later house about 1810–17; this places the estate within the movement of wealth extracted from enslaved labour into a Scottish landed property.<ref name="smith">Simon D. Smith, “Slavery's heritage footprint: links between British country houses and St Vincent plantations, 1814–1834,” in Madge Dresser and Andrew Hann, eds., ''Slavery and the British Country House'' (English Heritage, 2013), p. 62, [https://historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/slavery-and-british-country-house/slavery-british-country-house-web/ digitised volume].</ref>

He died at Montgreenan on 19 April 1827 according to Ayrshire accounts.<ref name="gazetteer">[https://aanhsorg.files.wordpress.com/2020/05/gazetteer-of-ayrshire.pdf ''Gazetteer of Ayrshire'']; cited as a historical account.</ref><ref name="hotel">[https://web.archive.org/web/20050924143852/http://montgreenanhotel.com/welcome_history.asp Archived Montgreenan Hotel history]; cited as a historical account.</ref> A related UCL entry describes Dr Robert Glasgow as “d. 1828” while citing an October 1828 registration. The primary Scottish papers have not yet been inspected, so this difference is not resolved here.<ref name="robertson">[https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/27300 “Robert Glasgow late Robertson”], ''Legacies of British Slavery'', UCL; [https://wwwdepts-live.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/27300 accessible mirror]; citing SC6/44/4/1 and an October 1828 registration; consulted 10 September 2026.</ref>

== Family and succession ==

An 1803 trust, summarized by UCL's ''Legacies of British Slavery'' database and cited there to Scottish record SC6/44/4, made a £200 legacy to Robert's “reputed natural mulatto son” John and lawful issue, and £500 to his “reputed natural daughter” Emilia and lawful issue. It also made legacies to Robert and James, described as reputed natural sons of Robert's late brother James. UCL identifies Anne as Robert's natural daughter and reports that Anne and her husband Robert Robertson succeeded under a Glasgow-name condition.<ref name="ucl">[https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/2146643739 “Dr Robert Glasgow”], ''Legacies of British Slavery'', UCL; [https://wwwdepts-live.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/2146643739 accessible mirror]; citing SC6/44/4, T71/493 pp. 591–592 and T71/495 p. 54; consulted 10 September 2026.</ref>

The three profiles currently attached as Robert's children are [[Glasgow-2952|John Glasgow]], [[Glasgow-3789|Amelia (Glasgow) Wilson]] and [[Glasgow-2874|Anne Glasgow]]. The UCL summary supplies names that may correspond to them, but the original trust and St Vincent registers have not yet been read for this biography. They therefore do not establish the profile identities: that its John was [[Glasgow-2952|John Glasgow]], that its Emilia was [[Glasgow-3789|Amelia (Glasgow) Wilson]], or that its Anne was [[Glasgow-2874|Anne Glasgow]]. They also do not establish the maternal identifications recorded on those profiles, that Mary, Adam, Eve, Peter and James formed John's family, or that other Caribbean bearers of the Glasgow surname descended from Robert.

James Paterson's nineteenth-century account states that Robert died without issue and describes the Robertson surname condition. Its childlessness statement conflicts with the later UCL trust summary; the original trust is needed to determine the scope and meaning of each account.<ref name="paterson">James Paterson, ''History of the County of Ayr'', vol. II, pp. 252–253, [https://archive.org/details/historyofcountyo02pateuoft/page/252/mode/2up Internet Archive].</ref>

== Research Notes ==

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Robert_Glasgow Wikipedia’s “Sir Robert Glasgow” article] is a tertiary overview and does not establish the relationships discussed above. Likewise, the 1679 wreck of the ''Croune'' is not evidence about this Robert, who was born in 1747.<ref>[https://drmarkjardine.wordpress.com/2016/12/10/beyond-orkneys-fatal-shore-the-wreck-of-the-croune-10-december-1679-history-scotland/ Mark Jardine, “Beyond Orkney's Fatal Shore: the wreck of the ''Croune'', 10 December 1679”].</ref>
